blocks.text: Do people turn silently read items into a sound-based code? **Conrad (1964)** and **Murray (1968)** tested this with lists of letters that either sounded alike or sounded different, and people had to click the letters back in the order shown. On some trials they also said 'one, two, three, four' out loud, which is **articulatory suppression**, and on others they stayed quiet.
children: Sound-alike lists are harder to hold in order, even when read silently.

blocks.text: **Similar-sounding lists were recalled worse**, even though nobody spoke them. When suppression occupied the speech system on visually presented lists, the cost disappeared. This shows that people **recode what they see into a speech-based form**, which is the basis of the **phonological loop**.
children: The mix-up is about similar sound, not similar look. A visual code would instead confuse look-alikes such as E and F.

blocks.text: Does what you already know about words in long-term memory change how well you hold them in short-term memory? **Roodenrys et al. (2002)** compared words from **large neighborhoods**, like cat, with words from **small neighborhoods**, like hippopotamus, and measured how well people recalled the words in order.
children: A neighbor differs by one letter or one sound. A word that only means the same thing is not a neighbor.

blocks.text: **Large neighborhood words were recalled better** in short-term memory tasks. So long-term knowledge of words helps short-term recall, and **memory span is not a pure measure of short-term capacity**.

What happens to short-term memory when rehearsal is blocked? In the **Brown-Peterson task**, **Peterson and Peterson (1959)** had people study consonants and then count backwards for varying lengths of time before recalling them. The counting kept them from rehearsing.
children: The longer the distraction, the worse the recall.

blocks.text: Because counting is so unlike remembering letters, the researchers judged interference an unlikely cause and concluded that short-term memory loses information through **decay** unless it is rehearsed. This challenged the view, following McGeoch's (1932) critique, that forgetting is due to interference.
children: Decay is the researchers' conclusion, and Keppel and Underwood (1962) are cited for an alternative based on interference.

blocks.text: Is memory better when a list is heard than when it is read? The **modality effect** compares lists that were heard with lists read silently, using digits in random order, and looks at memory for the last one or two items.
children: The advantage is for the last items of the list, not the whole list.

blocks.text: Heard lists gave **better memory for the final items**, and lip-read or silently mouthed lists show it too. The favored explanation (**Neath and Surprenant, 2003**) is that hearing adds information about how the list sounded, which helps the final items. The effect strongly influenced ideas about **sensory memory**, a back-up store of raw, unanalyzed sensory input.

People can report only a small part of a brief display. Is that limit in perception or in recall? **Sperling (1960)** varied whether a cue telling observers which part to report came right after the display or after a delay, and measured how much of the cued part they reported.
children: The limit is in reporting, not in what people saw.

blocks.text: With an **immediate cue**, observers reported the cued part almost perfectly, so a **sensory (iconic) store** briefly held nearly all of the display. With a **delayed cue**, performance fell toward the usual limit. The store is very short-lived, so the real limit is the time needed to report.
How are order errors in recall patterned? Nothing was compared across groups here. Instead, each recalled letter's placed position was compared with its true position in the list.

Items were **usually placed in the correct position**, and when they were not, the errors were **systematic**: the item landed in an **adjacent position**. So people keep approximate position information.
children: Order errors are not random, and scoring only percent correct hides this pattern.

blocks.text: Do mental images behave like real images? Self-reports of imagery are unreliable, because it is impossible to tell whether the images differ or only the descriptions. So researchers use tasks that require imagery. **Shepard and Metzler (1971)** showed two block shapes, one turned relative to the other, and people judged whether they were the same shape or mirror images.
children: Self-reports of imagery cannot be trusted, so the task itself must require imagery.

blocks.text: The **larger the turn, the longer the response**, at a constant rate. People were mentally rotating one shape, which suggests **mental images are much like real images**. This influenced theories of mental representation.

Do people judge probability by the rules of probability or by heuristics? **Tversky and Kahneman (1983)** and **Shafir, Smith, and Osherson (1990)** had people rate how likely descriptions of a person were to fit single professions or activities versus combinations of them.
children: A combination can never be more likely than either part alone.

blocks.text: People sometimes rated a combination as **more likely** than one of its parts, which is the **conjunction fallacy**. This points to **heuristics** that trade accuracy for speed: usually good enough, but sometimes wrong.

Do people test abstract rules as well as familiar ones? **Wason and Shapiro (1971)** compared abstract rules, with letters and numbers, to thematic rules, like borrowing a car, and recorded which cards people chose to turn over.
children: The 3 can only confirm the rule, while the 7 could falsify it.

blocks.text: For the rule 'If a card has a D on one side, it has a 3 on the other', most people chose **D and 3** instead of the better test, **D and 7**. **Thematic rules were much easier**. With relevant experience people test a rule well, while abstract rules force them to use logic alone.

Can wording or context change choices between options that are otherwise equivalent? **Kahneman and Tversky (1982)** summarized many such **framing effects**. In classic framing research (Tversky and Kahneman), the same choice is presented with gain wording or with loss wording, and people choose which option they prefer.
children: The situations are otherwise equivalent, so only the wording differs.

blocks.text: **Gain wording led to the sure option** and **loss wording to the gamble**. So choices can follow the framing and not the substance.

Do people have good intuition about the probability of combined events? In the **Monty Hall 3 Door problem**, you pick one of three doors, and the host, who always plays fair this way, opens a no-prize door. The question is whether you should stay or switch.
children: The two remaining doors are not equally likely.

blocks.text: Many people think it makes no difference, which is incorrect. **Switching wins about two-thirds of the time** and staying about one-third. Your first pick keeps its 1 in 3 chance, so the 2 in 3 held by the other two doors moves to the one remaining door.

Do risky choices depend on whether outcomes are seen as gains or losses? In research on **prospect theory**, **Kahneman and Tversky** had people pick between a guaranteed outcome and a gamble, where the guaranteed outcome could be a gain or a loss.
children: Losses lead to gambling, not caution.

blocks.text: With gains, people **avoided risk** and took the sure thing. With losses, people **sought risk** and took the gamble. So decisions about risk depend on how outcomes are perceived, not only on the objective odds.

title: German & Defeyter (2000): Immunity to functional fixedness in young children

blocks.text: Do young children get stuck on an object's usual function, which is **functional fixedness**? **German and Defeyter (2000)** compared children who had first seen a box used as a container with children who had not, and measured how long they took to offer the box as a support. They tested 5-, 6- and 7-year-olds.

Children aged 6 and 7 were **slower** after seeing the box as a container. The 5-year-olds were not slowed and were even faster than the older children. Younger children seem to have a more fluid idea of function, so one demonstrated use did not lock the object in.
children: Younger children did better here, not worse.

title: Leist et al. (2022): Irrelevant speech impairs serial recall of verbal but not spatial items

blocks.text: Does speech that people are told to ignore hurt only verbal items, or spatial items too? **Leist and colleagues (2022)** had third graders and adults recall the order of verbal or spatial items while hearing quiet, steady-state or changing-state speech.

Speech **hurt verbal recall but not spatial recall**, in both children and adults. Changing-state speech hurt more than steady-state speech, but only for verbal items. The effect is specific to verbal material, which fits **phonological interference** better than attention-capture or changing-state accounts.
children: The irrelevant speech effect depends on the material being verbal.

title: Morrison & Richmond (2020): Offloading items from memory

blocks.text: Who offloads items from memory, and does it help? **Morrison and Richmond (2020)** studied **cognitive offloading**, using actions like writing things down to reduce mental demands (Risko and Gilbert, 2016). A no-choice block allowed memory only, while a choice block allowed pen and paper, with lists of different lengths.

**Offloading improved memory**, especially at high loads, and people offloaded more as load grew. Low-capacity people were expected to offload more, but **memory ability did not predict who offloaded**. So offloading may be a compensatory strategy across abilities.

In the **bat-and-ball problem** (Frederick, 2005), a bat and ball cost $1.10 and the bat costs $1.00 more. The intuitive answer of 10 cents is wrong; the answer is 5 cents. Kahneman and Frederick (2002) called the error **unconscious attribute substitution**, and De Neys and colleagues (2013) found wrong reasoners were less confident than on a control version.

**Hoover and Healy (2019)** tested whether people unconsciously ignore 'more than', comparing the standard problem with a control version without it. They measured confidence and later recall and recognition of the wording. **Wrong reasoners mostly remembered 'more than'**, so it was not simply overlooked.
children: Substitution cannot be confirmed as the cause, so the authors prefer the term **error sensitivity**.

title: Giuliani et al. (2023): The joint effect of framing and defaults on choice behavior

blocks.text: What happens when the **framing effect** and the **default effect** act together? **Giuliani and colleagues (2023)** varied gain versus loss wording and also whether there was no default, a sure default or a risky default, in life-or-death and money scenarios. They measured whether people chose the sure or the risky option.

A **risky default raised risk taking**, a sure default did not raise risk aversion, and the framing and default effects were **additive**. In an exploratory question asked after the choice, people who thought the default was most rational followed it most.
children: That belief question came after the choice, so it may be a justification rather than a cause.

title: Chein et al. (2011) and Albert, Chein & Steinberg (2013): Peers and the adolescent brain

blocks.text: Why do adolescents take more risks with peers around? **Chein and colleagues (2011)** scanned adolescents, young adults and adults playing a driving game either alone or watched by friends, measuring risky driving choices and activity in reward and cognitive-control regions.

Adolescents **took more risks when watched**, with greater reward-region activity, while cognitive-control regions did not change with peers. The authors concluded the effect works mainly through **reward circuitry**. **Albert, Chein and Steinberg (2013)** argue that adolescents reason about risk like adults in the lab, and the peer context is what raises risk taking.
children: The peer context changes behavior, not the ability to reason about risk.
